User: I'm going through a legal process and need to organize my thoughts. The case involves nondisclosure agreement dispute. My lawyer is Lisa Park with Park Legal Group; we have proceedings at the federal district court. We're past the filing stage and waiting for the court calendar.. Opposing party: my former landlord. This is in King County, Washington. The contract was signed last year and they've since stopped performing. Can you help me figure out what to ask my attorney about what documents I should bring and what to say in the hearing? I want to be ready for the legal next steps.
Assistant: I can definitely help you organize what to bring and how to prepare questions and talking points so you and Lisa Park are ready for the next steps. I’m not a lawyer, so treat this as practical preparation and checklist guidance — you should run these items and any wording past Lisa for legal strategy and accuracy.

Key things to confirm with your attorney first
- What type of hearing is this? (status conference / motion hearing / preliminary injunction / evidentiary hearing / scheduling conference) — the format determines what to bring and whether you’ll speak/testify.
- Who will speak at the hearing (you, your lawyer, both)? Will you be asked to testify or only your attorney?
- Expected length and whether witnesses or exhibits will be admitted.
- Judge’s local practices or standing orders (how exhibits must be submitted, required exhibit lists, page limits, time limits).
- Whether the hearing will be in person or by video/phone and any tech requirements.
- Whether there are pre-hearing filings still due (briefs, proposed orders, exhibit lists).
Ask Lisa to summarize the legal standard the court will apply at the hearing and what burden of proof you must meet.

Documents and evidence to gather (physical and electronic)
Bring originals where available and 2–3 organized copies (one for you, one for Lisa, one for the court/opposing counsel), plus a labeled USB and PDF copies.
- The signed NDA (original and any signed amendments or related contracts).
- Any separate lease or landlord contract that overlaps with the NDA, if applicable.
- All communications with the landlord about the NDA and performance: emails, texts, letters, certified mail receipts, delivery confirmations, messages, and notes of phone calls (with dates/times and participants).
- Dates showing when the contract was signed and when performance stopped; a clear chronology/spreadsheet.
- Any written notices of breach you sent and landlord’s responses (notice to cure, demand letters).
- Documents showing performance on your side (if applicable) and actions you took to comply/mitigate.
- Financial records showing damages/losses: invoices, receipts, bank statements, cancelled checks, accounting summaries.
- Photos, screenshots, or other documentary evidence relevant to the dispute.
- Witness contact info and short written statements/declarations from witnesses who can corroborate timeline or facts (include dates they observed events).
- Copies of any police reports or official filings if relevant.
- Prior filings in this case and related case docket entries: complaint, answer, motions, declarations, exhibits previously filed, and any court orders already issued.
- Any drafts of the NDA or negotiation notes that show intent or interpretation (if helpful).
- Evidence of attempts to resolve/settle before or during litigation (emails, offers).
- Insurance policies or third-party documents if someone else may cover damages.
- Any expert reports or supporting analyses (if already retained).
Practical document prep
- Create an exhibit list (Exhibit 1, Exhibit 2, etc.) with short descriptions and dates.
- Bates-stamp or uniquely label each exhibit. Provide a table of contents for your binder.
- Create a one-page timeline of events and a one-page “what we seek” summary (damages/remedies requested).
- Prepare a short witness/contact sheet with names, phone/email, and short bullet of their expected testimony.

Questions to ask Lisa Park (use these in your meeting)
- What is our objective at the hearing? (e.g., scheduling, win a motion, get a temporary order)
- Which documents do you want certified/original? Which are ok as copies?
- Which exhibits will we present and how should they be numbered/formatted?
- Will I be required to testify? If so, what will you ask me and how should I respond?
- What are the strongest facts/arguments and what are our weaknesses?
- What defenses can the landlord raise and how should I respond if asked?
- Do we need witness declarations or affidavits filed beforehand?
- Any specific language you want me to use or avoid in court or in testimony?
- Are there pre-hearing filings I should prepare or review (proposed orders, proposed exhibit lists)?
- What is the plan if the judge asks for immediate relief or settlement?
- Do I have any deadlines for producing documents or discovery responses?
- Will you object to certain types of questioning or evidence — and how will that affect my testimony?
- Logistics: when and where to meet, arrival time for the hearing, dress, and courtroom protocol.

What to say in the hearing — short, clear, factual guidance
- If your lawyer will speak, coordinate a one-sentence opening for you (if you speak): “My name is [Your Name]; I am here because the landlord has stopped performing under the nondisclosure agreement signed on [date], and I request [specific relief].”
- When describing facts, use short, chronological statements: date — action — evidence. Example: “On March 14, 2025, I sent the landlord a written notice of breach (Exhibit 6). They did not respond. The landlord ceased performance on April 1, 2025 (see Exhibit 3).”
- Stick to verifiable facts, avoid speculation or emotional language (no “they intentionally…” unless you have evidence).
- If asked about damages, state the concrete amounts and point to supporting exhibits: “My documented damages total $X (Exhibit 12 — bank statements/invoices).”
- If you don’t know or don’t remember exact details, say so: “I don’t recall the exact time, but my records show [date/entry].” Don’t guess.
- If the judge or opposing counsel asks a question that might be harmful, consult Lisa in-court about whether to answer or invoke privilege; do not volunteer extraneous info.
- For cross-examination or tough questions, keep answers brief and responsive — one sentence when possible.
- Confirm with Lisa whether you should express willingness to negotiate or keep settlement discussions off-record.

Preparing testimony and practicing
- Work with Lisa to prepare a short script for direct testimony and practice it aloud. Keep it factual and in chronological order.
- Anticipate cross-examination: ask Lisa to run a mock cross with likely lines of attack and practice concise responses.
- Learn the exhibit numbers and where your key documents are in the binder so you can quickly reference them.
- Review common objections (relevance, hearsay, foundation) and know when Lisa may object on your behalf.

Courtroom logistics and etiquette
- Arrive early, bring ID, and have a backup copy of exhibits on a USB and in printed binder.
- Dress conservatively and professionally.
- Turn off phone. If remote, test video/audio and have a quiet, neutral background.
- Address the judge as “Your Honor” and wait for your lawyer to direct you when to speak.
- Keep notes minimal — a printed one-page timeline is fine — avoid reading long statements in court unless instructed.

Preservation and follow-up
- Preserve all texts/emails and don’t delete anything — take screenshots and export email threads (with metadata if possible).
- Do not communicate with the opposing party directly about the litigation without Lisa’s approval.
- Confirm which additional documents Lisa wants produced and by what date.
- Ask Lisa about deadlines for proposed orders, preliminary injunctions, discovery requests, and expert disclosures.

Sample one-page materials to bring to your meeting with Lisa
- One-page timeline of events (dates and one-line descriptions).
- One-page list of exhibits with brief descriptions and where originals are stored.
- One-page summary: “What happened,” “Why it breaches the NDA,” “What I want the court to do.”
- Contact list for witnesses and a list of documents you still need to find.

Next actions for you
1. Compile the documents listed above and create the exhibit list. 
2. Email Lisa (or bring this packet) and ask her the specific questions listed so you’re aligned on strategy.
3. Schedule a prep meeting with Lisa to review testimony and exhibits at least a few days before the hearing.
4. Preserve all communications and don’t communicate with the landlord about the case without counsel.

If you want, I can:
- Draft a one-page timeline template you can fill in;
- Draft an email to Lisa Park listing the documents and questions you want to confirm before the hearing;
- Create an exhibit checklist format you can print.

Which of those would you like me to prepare for you now?
